newsitem.title: FRANCE: Cook wants UK at EU heart with France, Germany.
newsitem.headline: Cook wants UK at EU heart with France, Germany.

text.p: British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook, in Paris on his first ministerial trip abroad, said on Wednesday he wanted Britain to have a "fresh start" and be one of the three leading players in Europe alongside France and Germany.
He said a new approach "will be good for Britain and it will be good for Europe" after Labour's election landslide swept away the Conservatives after 18 years in power.

"I want to make sure that Britain has a fresh start in Europe and that Britain joins France and Germany as the leading players," Cook told reporters after meeting French Socialist opposition leader Lionel Jospin.

Cook, who was installed last week, later met French Foreign Minister Herve de Charette and was to travel to Bonn to meet Foreign Minister Klaus Kinkel and opposition leaders for talks signalling an end to Britain's often antagonistic relationship with its continental partners.

Neither Cook nor Jospin, who met for about 30 minutes, would comment on the likelihood of Britain joining a single European currency. Labour has retained the right not to join and promised to hold a referendum before any such decision was taken.
He said that the French Socialists were Labour's "sister party" in France but declined to say who he wanted to win a snap parliamentary election in France on May 25-June 1.
Both France's ruling centre-right and Socialists, running neck-and-neck in opinion polls, have claimed the victory of the "New Labour" as a boost for their own side.
He said his decision to meet Jospin before a lunch with de Charette was "an issue of the timetable".
He added: "We have good relations with our sister party but we will work very closely with whomever the French people choose to govern them."
Jospin said he was encouraged by Labour's victory.

"We are sister parties and so we are in rather close cooperation in some issues," he said. Asked if Labour's victory would give the French Socialists extra momentum, he replied: "I have my own momentum."
French European Affairs Minister Michel Barnier praised what he called the new British government's very constructive approach towards the EU.
"We were not expecting a revolution, but we did expect a new climate. What we have felt so far is a new climate," he said.
He said it was a "very positive signal" that Britain had decided to be represented at ministerial level on talks on reviewing the workings of EU institutions ahead of enlargement.

"I am sure that (Prime Minister) Tony Blair has a more positive vision of Europe in the defence of British interests...He sees his country right in the middle of Europe and not on the fringe," he said.

The Labour government has said it will sign the Social Chapter of the Maastricht Treaty at the EU's Amsterdam summit in June and says ministers rather than civil servants will attend all future talks on European integration.

Britain has said it is unlikely that it will join the European single currency in the first wave. But it has said it will agree to more qualified majority voting in some policy areas and support a new employment chapter in a new EU treaty.
